title: Thinking in Reactor
description: Reactor asks you to think about UI in a new way. You don't create controls and then change them one property at a time. Instead, you write a function that describes what the screen should look like for the current state. When the state changes, Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) runs that function again and updates the real WinUI controls for you.

---
title: "Thinking in Reactor"
description: "Reactor asks you to think about UI in a new way. You don't create controls and then change them one property at a time. Instead, you write a function that describes what the screen should look like for the current state. When the state changes, Microsoft.UI.Reactor (Reactor) runs that function again and updates the real WinUI controls for you."
---

This page explains that model:
components, elements, hooks, the render cycle, data flow, keys, and effects.
Then it builds a small filterable product list step by step, so you can see
how the ideas fit together. The steps follow React's
[Thinking in React](https://react.dev/learn/thinking-in-react) guide. If you
know XAML and MVVM, read [Coming from XAML](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/xaml-developers) after this
page.

## The core ideas [#the-core-ideas]

| Idea | What it means | Learn more |
|------|---------------|------------|
| UI is a function of state | `Render()` returns the UI for the current state. You change state, not controls. | [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components) |
| Elements are descriptions | `TextBlock("Hi")` returns an immutable record. It is not a control. | [Reconciliation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation) |
| State lives in hooks | `UseState` keeps a value between renders. Call hooks in the same order on every render. | [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks) |
| A state change re-renders | A setter schedules a new render. The reconciler then patches only what changed. | [Reactivity Model](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reactivity-model) |
| Data flows down, events flow up | A parent passes props to a child. The child calls a callback to ask for a change. | [Components](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components#lifted-state) |
| Keys give identity | A key tells the reconciler which list item is which between renders. | [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections) |
| Effects are for side effects | `UseEffect` runs after a render, for work outside the UI tree. | [Effects and Lifecycle](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects) |

## UI is a function of state [#ui-is-a-function-of-state]

In code-behind, you find a control and change it: you set
`favoriteButton.Content` to new text in a click handler. In Reactor you don't
do that. You write a component. Its `Render()` method reads the current state
and returns a description of the UI. Reactor calls `Render()` again each time
the state changes.

```csharp
class FavoriteButton : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (isFavorite, setIsFavorite) = UseState(false);

        // Render describes the UI for the current state. No code here
        // reaches into the button to change its text.
        return Button(
            isFavorite ? "Remove from favorites" : "Add to favorites",
            () => setIsFavorite(!isFavorite));
    }
}
```

`UseState(false)` returns the current value and a setter. A click calls the
setter with the new value. Reactor then runs `Render()` again, and this time
`Render()` returns a button with the other text. No line of code changes the
button's text. You only change the state, and the UI follows.

## Elements describe, controls display [#elements-describe-controls-display]

`TextBlock(...)`, `Button(...)` and `VStack(...)` are factory methods. They
return *elements*. An element is a small, immutable C# record that describes
one piece of UI. It is cheap to create. It is not a WinUI control, and it is
not on screen.

```csharp
var title = TextBlock("Products");          // a record, not a control
var big = title.FontSize(28).Bold();        // a new record

// `title` is unchanged. Nothing is on screen yet: the reconciler
// creates the WinUI TextBlock only when an element is rendered.
return VStack(8, big, title);
```

- **Modifiers return new records.** `.FontSize(28)` and `.Bold()` work like a
  C# `with` expression. The original element does not change.
- **A new tree on every render is normal.** Elements are cheap, so `Render()`
  builds the whole tree each time. You don't need to keep old elements around.
- **The reconciler owns the controls.** It creates a WinUI control when an
  element first appears and updates that control on later renders. Don't keep
  your own reference to a control and change it. If you need the real control,
  for example to move focus, use an element ref (`UseElementRef`).

## What happens when state changes [#what-happens-when-state-changes]

Every update in Reactor follows the same cycle.

![The Reactor render cycle. A setter changes state, Render returns a new element tree, the reconciler diffs it against the old tree, and only the changed properties are patched on the WinUI controls. User input calls a setter again.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/thinking-in-reactor/render-cycle.svg)

1. **State changes.** Your code calls a setter, for example
   `setFilterText("pen")`. The setter compares the new value with the current
   one. If they are equal, nothing else happens.
2. **Render.** Reactor schedules a render. Several setter calls in the same
   event handler are batched into one render. `Render()` runs and returns a
   new element tree.
3. **Diff.** The reconciler walks the new tree and the old tree together. It
   matches each new element with the old element in the same place, or with
   the same key.
4. **Patch.** For a matched element, the reconciler sets only the properties
   that changed on the existing control. It creates controls for new elements
   and removes controls for elements that are gone. A text box the user is
   typing in stays the same WinUI control, so it keeps its focus.

A child component with props is skipped when its props are equal to last
time. [Reconciliation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation) explains the diff in depth, and
[Reactivity Model](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reactivity-model) explains setters and batching.

## Hooks hold state in call order [#hooks-hold-state-in-call-order]

Local variables in `Render()` are gone when the method returns. Hooks keep
values between renders. Reactor stores hook values in slots, in the order you
call the hooks: the first `UseState` call is slot 0, the second is slot 1, and
so on. So call every hook at the top of `Render()`, on every render, in the
same order. Never call a hook inside an `if`, a loop, or after an early
`return`.

```csharp
// Don't: a hook inside an if changes the slot of every hook after it.
public override Element Render()
{
    var (showDetails, setShowDetails) = UseState(false);
    if (showDetails)
    {
        var (note, setNote) = UseState(""); // REACTOR_HOOKS_001
    }
    return ...;
}
```

Call the hook every time, and use the condition when you build the elements.
The `REACTOR_HOOKS_001` analyzer warns about this at build time. At run time,
a changed hook order can throw a `HookOrderException`.
[Rules of Reactor](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/get-started/rules-of-reactor) lists all the rules.

Treat state values as immutable. To change a list in state, create a new list
and pass it to the setter. If you change the old list in place and pass the
same object back, the setter sees an equal value and does not re-render.

## Data flows down, events flow up [#data-flows-down-events-flow-up]

A component that takes input derives from `Component<TProps>`. `TProps` is
usually a record. The parent creates the child with
`Component<TChild, TProps>(props)`, and the child reads `this.Props`. A child
never changes its props.

When a child needs to change something its parent owns, the parent passes a
callback down as a prop, and the child calls it. Data goes down through props.
Requests for change go up through callbacks. This is *one-way data flow*. It
makes a value easy to trace: follow the props up until you reach the component
that owns the state. Step 6 of the worked example below shows this in code.

## Keys give list items an identity [#keys-give-list-items-an-identity]

When you render a list with `ForEach`, give each item a key with
`.WithKey(...)`. Use a stable id from your data, not the position in the list.
The reconciler uses the key to match old and new items. Without keys it
matches by position. Then, when you filter or sort, a row's control and its
component state stay at the same position and now belong to a different item.

The `REACTOR_DSL_001` analyzer warns when a `ForEach` item has no key. Items
whose type implements `IReactorKeyed` get their key from the data
automatically. See [Collections](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/collections) and
[Identity and Key](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation#identity-and-key).

## Effects are for side effects [#effects-are-for-side-effects]

`Render()` must be pure. It reads state and props and returns elements.
It does not write to files, call services, start timers, or log. That work
goes in `UseEffect`. An effect runs after the new UI is committed, and runs
again only when one of its dependencies changes.

```csharp
class SearchBox : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (query, setQuery) = UseState("");

        // A side effect: it talks to something outside the UI tree.
        // It runs after the render, and again only when `query` changes.
        UseEffect(() => Debug.WriteLine($"Searched for '{query}'"), query);

        return TextBox(query, setQuery, placeholderText: "Search...")
            .AutomationName("Search");
    }
}
```

Don't use an effect to compute a value from state. Compute it in `Render()`
instead. [Effects and Lifecycle](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/effects) covers cleanup, async work, and
dependency rules.

## Worked example: a filterable product list [#worked-example-a-filterable-product-list]

This example builds a product list with a search box and an "only in stock"
check box. The product data is a fixed list. In a real app it would come from
a service or a file.

```csharp
record Product(string Id, string Name, string Category, decimal Price, bool InStock);

static class Catalog
{
    public static readonly IReadOnlyList<Product> Products =
    [
        new("p1", "Notebook", "Paper", 4.50m, true),
        new("p2", "Sticky notes", "Paper", 2.00m, true),
        new("p3", "Printer paper", "Paper", 8.99m, false),
        new("p4", "Gel pen", "Writing", 1.50m, true),
        new("p5", "Highlighter", "Writing", 1.25m, false),
        new("p6", "Desk lamp", "Lighting", 24.00m, true),
    ];
}
```

### Step 1: Sketch the UI [#step-1-sketch-the-ui]

Start with a sketch of the screen. Then draw a box around each part that has
one job. Each box becomes a component.

![A sketch of the product catalog. An outer ProductCatalog box holds a SearchBar box, with a search text box and an in-stock check box, and a ProductList box with six ProductRow boxes. Out-of-stock product names are red.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/thinking-in-reactor/catalog-sketch.svg)

### Step 2: Break the UI into components [#step-2-break-the-ui-into-components]

The sketch gives four components:

```text
ProductCatalog          the whole page
├── SearchBar           the search text and the check box
└── ProductList         the products that match
    └── ProductRow      one product (one per item)
```

Use one component for one job. If a component starts to do two jobs, split
it. The smallest piece, `ProductRow`, takes one product as its props and
shows it. An out-of-stock name uses the `Theme.SystemCritical` color token, so
it reads well in light and dark themes.

```csharp
record ProductRowProps(Product Product);

class ProductRow : Component<ProductRowProps>
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var p = Props.Product;

        return HStack(12,
            TextBlock(p.Name)
                .Foreground(p.InStock ? Theme.PrimaryText : Theme.SystemCritical)
                .Width(160),
            TextBlock(p.Category).Foreground(Theme.SecondaryText).Width(100),
            TextBlock($"${p.Price:0.00}"));
    }
}
```

### Step 3: Build a static version [#step-3-build-a-static-version]

Build a version that shows the data but has no state yet. Pass the data down
with props. A static version is quick to write, and it shows the shape of the
UI before you add behavior.

```csharp
record SearchBarProps(string FilterText, bool InStockOnly);

class SearchBar : Component<SearchBarProps>
{
    public override Element Render() =>
        VStack(8,
            TextBox(Props.FilterText, placeholderText: "Search...")
                .AutomationName("Search products"),
            CheckBox(Props.InStockOnly, label: "Only show products in stock"));
}

record ProductListProps(IReadOnlyList<Product> Products);

class ProductList : Component<ProductListProps>
{
    public override Element Render() =>
        VStack(4,
            ForEach(Props.Products, p =>
                Component<ProductRow, ProductRowProps>(new(p)).WithKey(p.Id)));
}
```

```csharp
class ProductCatalog : Component
{
    public override Element Render() =>
        VStack(16,
            Component<SearchBar, SearchBarProps>(new("", false)),
            Component<ProductList, ProductListProps>(new(Catalog.Products))
        ).Padding(24);
}
```

`ProductList` keys each row with the product id. The text box has an
automation name so screen readers can announce it. A placeholder is not
enough, and the `REACTOR_A11Y_003` analyzer warns when a text box has no
accessible name. The search box and check box show values from props, but
they don't change anything yet.

### Step 4: Find the minimal state [#step-4-find-the-minimal-state]

State is data that changes over time and that you can't compute from other
data. Ask three questions about each piece of data:

| Data | Passed in or fixed? | Can be computed? | State? |
|------|---------------------|------------------|--------|
| The product list | Yes, fixed | No | No |
| The search text | No, the user types it | No | **Yes** |
| The check box value | No, the user sets it | No | **Yes** |
| The products that match | No | Yes, from the three items above | No |

So the minimal state is two values: the search text and the check box value.
Keep it that small. Every extra piece of state is something that can get out
of sync.

### Step 5: Decide where the state lives [#step-5-decide-where-the-state-lives]

For each piece of state:

1. Find every component that reads it.
2. Find their closest common parent.
3. Put the state there.

`SearchBar` shows both values, and `ProductList` filters with both values.
Their closest common parent is `ProductCatalog`, so the state goes there:

```csharp
class ProductCatalog : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        // The minimal state: two values the user can change.
        var (filterText, setFilterText) = UseState("");
        var (inStockOnly, setInStockOnly) = UseState(false);

        return VStack(16,
            Component<SearchBar, SearchBarProps>(new(filterText, inStockOnly)),
            Component<ProductList, ProductListProps>(
                new(Catalog.Products, filterText, inStockOnly))
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

`ProductList` now takes the two values as props and computes the matching
products during `Render()`. The filtered list is derived data, so it is not
stored in state:

```csharp
record ProductListProps(IReadOnlyList<Product> Products, string FilterText, bool InStockOnly);

class ProductList : Component<ProductListProps>
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        // Derived data: computed from props on every render, never stored.
        var visible = Props.Products
            .Where(p => p.Name.Contains(Props.FilterText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .Where(p => !Props.InStockOnly || p.InStock)
            .ToList();

        return VStack(4,
            visible.Count == 0
                ? TextBlock("No products match.").Foreground(Theme.SecondaryText)
                : ForEach(visible, p =>
                    Component<ProductRow, ProductRowProps>(new(p)).WithKey(p.Id)));
    }
}
```

The app now filters correctly when the state changes. But the state never
changes yet, because the text box and check box have no callbacks.

### Step 6: Add inverse data flow [#step-6-add-inverse-data-flow]

`SearchBar` can't change state that `ProductCatalog` owns. Instead,
`ProductCatalog` passes callbacks down, and `SearchBar` calls them when the
user types or clicks.

```csharp
record SearchBarProps(
    string FilterText,
    bool InStockOnly,
    Action<string> OnFilterTextChange,
    Action<bool> OnInStockOnlyChange);

class SearchBar : Component<SearchBarProps>
{
    public override Element Render() =>
        VStack(8,
            TextBox(Props.FilterText, Props.OnFilterTextChange, placeholderText: "Search...")
                .AutomationName("Search products"),
            CheckBox(Props.InStockOnly, Props.OnInStockOnlyChange,
                label: "Only show products in stock"));
}
```

```csharp
class ProductCatalog : Component
{
    public override Element Render()
    {
        var (filterText, setFilterText) = UseState("");
        var (inStockOnly, setInStockOnly) = UseState(false);

        return VStack(16,
            // The setters go down as callbacks. The child calls them to ask
            // the parent to change its state.
            Component<SearchBar, SearchBarProps>(
                new(filterText, inStockOnly, setFilterText, setInStockOnly)),
            Component<ProductList, ProductListProps>(
                new(Catalog.Products, filterText, inStockOnly))
        ).Padding(24);
    }
}
```

Here is what happens when the user types "pen":

1. The text box calls `Props.OnFilterTextChange("pen")`. That is
   `setFilterText`, so the state in `ProductCatalog` changes.
2. `ProductCatalog` renders again and passes new props to `SearchBar` and
   `ProductList`.
3. `ProductList` filters again and returns one row, for "Gel pen".
4. The reconciler matches rows by key. It keeps the "Gel pen" row and removes
   the rows that no longer match.

`UseState` setters keep the same identity on every render. That is why the
root can pass them straight into the props record: the record still compares
equal when the data is the same. A new lambda on every render would make the
props unequal every time. For that case, see
[Callback props and memoization](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components#callback-props-and-memoization).

> **Caveat:** A child component that derives from `Component<TProps>` re-renders when its
> props change or when its own state changes. Reactor compares the old and new
> props with `Equals()`. For a record, that compares field by field. A field of
> type `IReadOnlyList<T>` compares by reference, not by content. If a parent
> builds a new list on every render and passes it as a prop, the child re-renders
> every time, even when the items are the same. In this example
> `Catalog.Products` is the same object on every render, so `ProductList`
> re-renders only when the search text or the check box changes. A component
> without props (`Component`) does not re-render when its parent does. It
> re-renders only from its own state.

## Patterns [#patterns]

### Lift state to the closest common parent [#lift-state-to-the-closest-common-parent]

When two components need the same value, move the state up to their closest
common parent and pass it down as props, as step 5 does. The
[Lifted state](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/components#lifted-state) pattern and the
[master-detail recipe](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/recipes/master-detail) show the same idea with a
shared selection.

### Derive, don't store [#derive-dont-store]

If you can compute a value from props or state, compute it in `Render()`.
`ProductList` filters on every render instead of keeping a filtered list in
state. For a slow computation, wrap it in `UseMemo` with the values it depends
on. See [Hooks](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/hooks).

### Pass setters down as callbacks [#pass-setters-down-as-callbacks]

A child that edits a parent's value takes the value and a callback in its
props. Pass the `UseState` setter itself when no extra logic is needed. Name
the callback for what happened, for example `OnFilterTextChange`.

### Keep components small [#keep-components-small]

A component should do one job. Small components are easier to read and test,
and a component that receives the same props is skipped during a render.

## Common Mistakes [#common-mistakes]

### Storing derived data in state [#storing-derived-data-in-state]

```csharp
// Don't: the filtered list is a copy that must be kept in sync.
var (filterText, setFilterText) = UseState("");
var (visible, setVisible) = UseState(Catalog.Products);
UseEffect(() => setVisible(Filter(Catalog.Products, filterText)), filterText);
```

This renders twice for each change: once with the old list, and again after
the effect sets the new list. Compute the list in `Render()` instead, as
`ProductList` does in step 5.

### Copying props into state [#copying-props-into-state]

```csharp
// Don't: the initial value is used only on the first render.
var (text, setText) = UseState(Props.FilterText);
```

`UseState` reads its argument only when the component first mounts. Later
changes to `Props.FilterText` are ignored. Read the prop directly, or lift the
state to the parent that owns it.

### Changing state in place [#changing-state-in-place]

```csharp
// Don't: the same list object is passed back, so nothing re-renders.
items.Add(newItem);
setItems(items);
```

The setter compares the new value with the old one, finds the same object,
and skips the render. Create a new list instead, for example
`setItems([.. items, newItem])`. The `REACTOR_HOOKS_010` analyzer flags this
pattern.

### Using the list index as a key [#using-the-list-index-as-a-key]

```csharp
// Don't: after filtering, index 0 is a different product.
ForEach(visible, (p, i) => Component<ProductRow, ProductRowProps>(new(p)).WithKey(i.ToString()))
```

Keys must follow the data, not the position. Use an id from the item, such as
`p.Id`. See [Using array index as a key](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/reconciliation#using-array-index-as-a-key).

## Tips [#tips]

- Start with a static version, then add state. It is easier to see which data
  really changes.
- Keep state minimal. If you can compute a value, don't store it.
- Keep `Render()` fast and free of side effects. It can run many times.
- Read the analyzer warnings. `REACTOR_HOOKS_001`, `REACTOR_DSL_001`,
  `REACTOR_HOOKS_010` and `REACTOR_A11Y_003` catch the mistakes on this page
  when you build.
- Give every input control a header or an automation name.
